title: The Khalsa shall rule
hook: a couplet after Ardas speaks of the Khalsa ruling; Sikhs understand it in several ways, from justice to spiritual sovereignty

segments.voice: Yesterday, langar in hard times: deg, the cooking pot, before the sword. Your line was share it anyway. What did you split that you'd usually keep? Day eight hundred eighty-one.

The Ardas is over. The congregation is still standing, hands folded. And then the whole room sings a short couplet together, loud and steady. It opens with three words in Punjabi: raj karega Khalsa. The Khalsa shall rule. For a visitor hearing it for the first time, it can land with a jolt. Rule over whom? Rule how? Those are fair questions, and Sikhs themselves answer them in more than one way. Today: the Khalsa shall rule.
screen: `AFTER THE ARDAS, A SUNG COUPLET.` → `RAJ KAREGA KHALSA.` → `RULE OVER WHOM? RULE HOW?`

segments.voice: Start with where it comes from. The couplet isn't in the Guru Granth Sahib. Tradition attributes it to Guru Gobind Singh, and it's recorded in one of the old codes of Sikh conduct. Its next lines say, in paraphrase, that none will stay defiant, that the ones who wandered in misery will come together, and that those who take shelter will be safe. Tradition says it was sung through the hunted century by people with a price on their heads. That's the first way Sikhs hear it: a promise of sovereignty, said aloud at the very moment it looked impossible, and later remembered when Sikh chiefs did hold the land. The second way is justice. Guru Arjan, in the Guru Granth Sahib, describes the kind of rule he means. Here in paraphrase: by the merciful one's command, no one pushes another around, no one hurts another, and everyone lives at ease. He calls it halemi raj, a gentle rule. Some readers hear raj karega Khalsa through that line: a rule where nobody is crushed. The third way turns inward. Khalsa can mean the pure, those who belong directly to the Guru. In this reading, the first kingdom to be ruled is the self: anger, greed, ego, fear. A person who can't rule their own temper isn't ready to rule anything else. These readings don't cancel each other out. Sikhs hold them side by side, and different gurdwaras and teachers lean different ways. But the third one is the one anyone can try on today. Rule yourself first.
screen: `A PROMISE SUNG WHILE HUNTED.` · `HALEMI RAJ: A GENTLE RULE.` · `THE FIRST KINGDOM IS THE SELF.` · `READINGS HELD SIDE BY SIDE.` · then, large: `RULE YOURSELF FIRST.`

segments.voice: Two minutes in your own small kingdom. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself one plain question: what in me tends to take over? Maybe it's temper in traffic, the phone at midnight, the urge to win every argument, worry that runs the whole morning. Name just one. Then picture the next time it rises, and picture yourself, for one breath, choosing what happens next. Not crushing it. Just being the one in charge. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.

halemi raj, the gentle rule Guru Arjan describes, where no one pushes another around and everyone lives at ease. Sikhs hear it in the couplet sung after the Ardas, alongside sovereignty and ruling one's own self. Today's word.
Your line: rule yourself first. Today, when the thing you named starts to take over, take one breath and make the next move yours. Day eight hundred eighty-one.
